📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 upcoming EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, upcoming data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico.
  • Recent findings suggest that ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition.
  • Sources indicate that “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Recent findings suggest that ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

Sources indicate that “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

According to recent reports, the SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

It has been revealed that considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

Before You Plan Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.
  • By this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving.
  • In a recent development, will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

By this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving. We’re discussing who’s coming, who’s bringing what, and whether people prefer the canned or fresh cranberry sauce. We may also be planning conversations that haven’t happened.

In a recent development, will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet? Will our parenting become a topic of discussion? Will we spend another holiday doing the work while everyone else watches football?

It has been revealed that I have written about the friction that can accompany family gatherings. As Thanksgiving approaches again, I keep wondering would it would look like to prepare for the family dynamics as thoughtfully as we prepare for the meal.

In a recent development, think about the moment you’re most concerned about. Perhaps it’s a particular question, a familiar disagreement, or the expectation that you’ll organize everything. Now consider what you’re predicting. Are you anticipating a situation that happens regularly? Or are you imagining several possible arguments and preparing a response to each one? Past experiences give us useful information, but mentally replaying an argument doesn’t necessarily give us a useful plan.

Try making the concern specific: “I’m worried someone will comment on my career decision.” Then identify a response you would feel comfortable using: “I’m comfortable with my decision, and I’m not looking for advice about it today.” You may still feel uncomfortable and dread having the conversation but having a response ready simply gives you somewhere to begin.

Sources indicate that we often approach holidays with goals that depend on other people, like everyone will get along, no one will make an insensitive comment, or everyone will appreciate the effort. Those hopes are understandable, but they’re also difficult to guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that consider a few decisions you can make yourself. How long will you stay? Which preparations can you reasonably take on? What will you do if a conversation becomes uncomfortable? You might decide to visit for dessert rather than spend the entire day. You might ask someone else to bring the side dishes. You might arrange transportation so you can leave when you’re ready.

These decisions deserve space alongside the grocery list.

If a familiar pattern bothers you, consider whether there’s a request you can make before the gathering. For example, if you usually manage the meal and cleanup, “I need more help this year” is a starting point. A more specific request gives others a clearer way to participate: “Can you handle the dishes after dinner, including putting the leftovers away?”.

According to recent reports, the same applies to traditions. If the usual schedule no longer works for your household, raise that issue while looks are being made. Others may be disappointed. You can acknowledge that disappointment while still explaining what you can offer.

In an uncomfortable moment, finding the right words can be difficult. Choose language that sounds like something you would actually say. For an intrusive question: “I don’t have anything I want to share about that.” For unsolicited advice: “I’ll ask if I need suggestions.” For a conversation you want to leave: “I’m going to step away for a few minutes.”.

Recent findings suggest that A prepared phrase won’t determine how another person responds. It can help you communicate your own decision more clearly.

Preparation can also include thinking about what you’re looking forward to: Is there someone you’d like to spend time with? A recipe you want to learn? A game, walk, or family story you’d enjoy sharing? Make a little room for that experience rather than assuming it will happen once everything else is finished.

Once you’re home after the gathering, give yourself a fair assessment of the day. One awkward exchange doesn’t have to define the entire gathering. You can appreciate the parts you enjoyed and think honestly about what you’d change next time.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving takes preparation. Along with deciding what belongs on the table, we can decide what we have the time, energy, and willingness to bring to it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slate Auto is not subtle about keeping its electric truck simple and analog whenever possible. It has hand-crank windows, no carpeting to speak of, and—perhaps most significantly for a car launching in the back half of the 2020s—no central screen. That means navigation duties are probably going to fall to your phone, but Slate is happy to offer another option on its online store. They call it a physical GPS, but you probably know it by another name. The familiar-looking new product available on the Slate website is simply a Slate-branded Rand McNally Road Atlas.

Industry observers note that in other words, maps. Slate is selling maps.

Sources indicate that slate built its Truck—that is its official product name—around the idea that a driver will be using their phone for navigation and entertainment, so the Road Atlas offering is mostly a novelty. Still, it is a Slate-branded book of maps covering Canada, Mexico, and the United States. That is useful enough that it might convince one or two dedicated analog buyers to actually choose to navigate their Slate Trucks through the world this way, at least once or twice for the novelty.

The Slate store lists the atlas for $30, and notes that it is “limited edition.” (We will note that the same apparent atlas without the Slate markings and markup costs $19.99 on Amazon.) Slate’s planned products range from starting prices of just under $25,000 to just over $32,000, depending on which of three customizable body styles a buyer picks. Add in $30 for a “Screenless GPS” and you can get yourself across the continent with ease, one 205-mile charge at a time.

#5242. Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (464 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Robo-frog swims with liquid crystal muscles powered by light

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (464 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts.
  • Industry observers note that the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies.
  • “I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, remarked in a profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

Industry observers note that the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, remarked in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That stated, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

It has been revealed that “In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” mentioned Ryberg.

It has been revealed that the final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination promptly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a new way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

#5241. Latest Update: Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • Sources indicate that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • Industry observers note that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a upcoming-generation Model Y in traffic.

Sources indicate that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

Industry observers note that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

Sources indicate that this isn’t fresh in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

According to recent reports, A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Recent findings suggest that now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Recent findings suggest that tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

According to recent reports, since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual notes about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

Industry observers note that in other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

It has been revealed that the penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

According to recent reports, the Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

Industry observers note that we’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

According to recent reports, people have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

Industry observers note that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

Our Long-Term Ram 1500 Taught Us to Love Hurricanes

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, for 2025, Ram pulled the Hemi V-8 from the lineup.
  • Over 40,000 miles, our Significant Horn 4x4 model was a six-passenger, 5765-pound workhorse for all manner of tasks: towing trailers, swallowing luggage, devouring interstate miles, and hauling the kind of oversize objects people buy because they have access to a pickup, a credit card, and a Costco membership.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our expectations for the Ram 1500 are well established. This being the third 1500 of the current generation we’ve put through a long-term test, the only real question mark was under the hood.

According to recent reports, for 2025, Ram pulled the Hemi V-8 from the lineup. In its place came the Hurricane: a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six making 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque in its base form. Sure, that’s more power than the Hemi produced, but some buyers hold V-8-powered full-size trucks as a fundamental truth, right next to basic arithmetic and gravity. These folks would probably dismiss the Ram’s twin-turbo six outright. Their loss.

Over 40,000 miles, our Significant Horn 4x4 model was a six-passenger, 5765-pound workhorse for all manner of tasks: towing trailers, swallowing luggage, devouring interstate miles, and hauling the kind of oversize objects people buy because they have access to a pickup, a credit card, and a Costco membership.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 28539.

With the Hurricane, the Ram proved smooth, strong, and surprisingly sophisticated, like a BMW wearing Carhartt. We loved its power too. Our initial testing logged 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and the quarter-mile in 13.6 seconds at 100 mph. That’s serious pace for a crew-cab pickup on Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires, and it was 1.3 seconds quicker to 60 mph than the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered 2019 Ram 1500 we ran through a 40,000-mile test. Our 2025 example repeated its 60-mph time at 40,000 miles, though its quarter-mile effort slipped a little to 13.8 seconds at 96 mph. Still, leave it in rear-drive mode, and the traction-control light will occasionally flicker during moderate freeway acceleration in the wet. That is not a complaint.

Indeed, driving the Ram 1500 leads to few complaints, which is why it’s been on our 10Best list eight times. The 1500, with its four-corner coil-spring suspension, rode with the calm authority that has long separated this truck from its rear-leaf-spring competitors, cruising and towing with the ease of a long-legged Clydesdale at a trot and making you wonder why other pickups don’t ride this well.

The Ram was a happy mile eater, as the optional 33.0-gallon fuel tank regularly demonstrated more than 500 miles of indicated range after a fill-up. The cabin was a great place to while away the hours. Ram has been doing excellent truck interiors long enough that the surprise has worn off, but the usefulness remains. The front bench gave us seating for six and a healthy dose of nostalgia, the rear seat offered limo-like sprawl-out space, and the front armrest placed a hand naturally in line with the shifter and stereo controls.

Our most vocal complaints fell on the large mirrors from the Trailer-Tow Group package. They were fantastic when there was a trailer behind you and a nuisance when there wasn’t, blocking entire cars at roundabouts and requiring chicken-like head bobbing to see around them.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 28539.

Worse, the mirrors fold and extend manually on this near-$70,000 truck (power-extending and folding mirrors are available). Also missing is passive entry, because Ram limited its availability for 2025 to Laramie and higher trims, and we didn’t notice when we ordered ours. Oops. We did go for the Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, which adds a 12.0-inch touchscreen, heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, navigation, and a larger digital display in the instrument cluster. Keyless entry should be part of that package. Having to get the key fob out to unlock the doors would be acceptable on a contractor-spec truck. Or in the year 2015.

Remote start was present but inspired its own confusion. It would not operate with the fuel tank at a quarter full or below, which seems overly cautious when a quarter tank is over eight gallons and could get you halfway to Chicago from Ann Arbor. A considerable delay from when you double-tap the button to when the engine starts raised doubts that it had worked. This is especially charming on a winter day when your spouse is standing beside the truck holding a toddler who has entered the combat phase of development.

It has been revealed that fuel economy was the other great qualifier. We averaged 15 mpg; our long-term 2019 Ram V-8 managed 14. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, the upcoming Ram returned 18 mpg while the V-8 logged 17. A real-world 1-mpg improvement isn’t the efficiency promise we were told would justify ditching two cylinders. Instead, the Hurricane delivered improved acceleration, which is arguably a better bargain.

In a recent development, the last great frustration was our dealer’s service center and how often we visited it. Scheduled maintenance came at 10,000-mile intervals. Each appointment at Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor was more expensive than we expected. Examples included $60 for a cabin air filter that retails online for roughly half that and added services that aren’t in the owner’s manual.

High prices didn’t end at the service department either. A plastic clamp and a section of railing broke on our trifold tonneau cover, likely from one of us loading the bed with more enthusiasm than finesse. A replacement tonneau cost $2200 at the parts counter, which is curious considering it was a $550 factory option. We replaced the broken pieces instead, but even those bits cost $148. All in, our out-of-pocket maintenance costs amounted to $829.

Sources indicate that the unscheduled visits were more troubling, because there were five of them. When the truck arrived, it couldn’t tow until we replaced the integrated trailer-control module, and that required a return visit once the part arrived. Around 18,000 miles, the forward-collision warning stopped working. At roughly 30,000, a wastegate actuator failed, throwing a check-engine light and effectively shutting off the turbochargers. Near the end, the infotainment system needed a dealer visit for an revision. None of these problems stranded us or created a repair bill, but considered together, they made us wonder about reliability outside the warranty.

The Ram stayed beloved anyway, because the driving experience and utility outweighed the annoyances. Ram revived the Hemi for 2026. It’s as charming as ever and sounds amazing, and anyone claiming immunity to a V-8 pickup should have to explain themselves under oath. The smooth turbo six-cylinder is more efficient (slightly), powerful, and modern in ways you feel every time it comes onto the boost.

We entered this test wondering whether a six-cylinder Ram could make us forget the V-8. Forty thousand miles later, we remember it just fine. We just wouldn’t order one.

“The peaceful ride of a luxury car, the acceleration of a sports car, and the cornering ability of, well, a pickup.”—Tony Quiroga.

Industry observers note that “I drove five hours in a snowstorm. In 4WD Auto, the Ram 1500 handled the challenge with ease.” —Collin Morgan.

“I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram.” —Caleb Miller.

“I drove about 500 miles with the truck unloaded, then 500 miles pulling a side-by-side, and can say this just might be the perfect road-trip vehicle.”—Dave VanderWerp.

“Nix the tow mirrors and add a proximity key, and you’ve got a practically perfect full-size truck.” —Greg Fink.

“Despite creating forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas, the tow mirrors were great for seeing behind a trailer during a seven-hour trip.” —Jack Fitzgerald.

“There is no better half-ton truck for a long-haul road trip.” —Eric Stafford.

Industry observers note that our two regrets of our long-term Ram’s build are the lack of passive entry and the Dumbo towing mirrors. Ram now includes the former item on the Massive Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, but ditching the latter means going without the helpful, but unnecessary, surround-view camera. So, scratching the mirrors but keeping everything else the same results in a 2027 price of $69,985. It might be the perfect non-luxury-spec pickup.

It has been revealed that thirty thousand miles in, associate news editor Caleb Miller offered perhaps the strangest compliment a pickup truck has ever received. "I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram," he wrote in the logbook.

According to recent reports, at peace. In a pickup truck. That's either a testament to this truck's deeply soothing character or evidence that Miller should talk to someone. But he's not alone. Praise for the Ram has run throughout its logbook since the truck demonstrated up. There's a steady stream of staffers angling for the keys each week.

So, it's a real shame that the truck can't stay out of the service department.

Managing testing editor David Beard started the Ram one morning on a road trip and climbed in to find the check-engine light glowing with the quiet menace of a "we need to talk" text. The truck seemed to be running fine, so Beard made the three-hour drive home. It was somewhere along I-75, as the Ram began downshifting on hills that had never previously required it, that he realized the Hurricane inline-six engine wasn't making full power. A scan tool confirmed his suspicion: a wastegate-actuator fault. The turbos had effectively clocked out.

The dealership unplugged the actuator, checked the wiring from the control module to the wastegate, found it all in order, and replaced the actuator. The fault cleared and hasn't returned. It's the sort of repair that is both reassuringly straightforward and philosophically loaded. Nobody who ever owned a factory Hemi V-8 has Googled "wastegate actuator." The Hemi just existed, doing its thing.

Elsewhere in the durability report, the trifold tonneau cover suffered a structural failure when both a plastic clamp and a piece of railing broke; the likely result of a load shifting in the bed or someone being less than delicate while loading it. The result: One morning on the freeway, the cover began performing a convincing impression of a sailboat. We removed it. An OEM replacement carries an MSRP of $2200 from Mopar. That's four times the $550 option price on our 2025 model's original window sticker, so we'll attempt to repair the broken clamp and rail piece first. Stay tuned.

These problems join a growing list. The Ram arrived needing its integrated trailer-control module replaced to fix an intermittent trailer-light issue that prevented us from towing. Later, a malfunctioning forward-collision system required a dealer visit to swap the long-range radar module. These aren't catastrophic on their own, and both were covered under warranty, but they add up to a truck that has required four unscheduled service visits in 30,000 miles.

What the Ram does between those visits, though, still makes the case.

Recent findings suggest that vehicle testing director Dave VanderWerp covered 500 miles unloaded and another 500 miles pulling a side-by-side. His verdict? "This may be the perfect road-trip vehicle," he wrote. "The air suspension is great for levelling out the load, and somehow it knows the trailer is 20 feet long and the blind-spot-monitoring system adjusts accordingly.".

According to recent reports, vanderWerp then noted with remarkable casualness that the truck was very stable while towing at 80 mph, and it got 10 mpg in the process. Hey, this is the U.S.A., and we have places to go.

Industry observers note that he was less convinced by the Trailer Reverse Steering Control system, consisting of a knob on the dash that lets you steer the trailer while the truck handles the wheel. "Seems much easier and straightforward to just steer myself," he wrote, arguing that sometimes the best user interface is a steering wheel and a functioning human brain.

In a recent development, but for all its towing prowess and sophistication, we are baffled by the amnesia of the Tow mode button. If the truck is smart enough to detect a 20-foot trailer, it should be smart enough to remember you'd like to be in Tow mode when you restart the engine with the trailer still attached. Instead, it resets the drive mode every ignition cycle.

Fuel economy, meanwhile, has regressed. After climbing from 14 mpg at the introduction to 16 mpg at our 20,000-mile revision, the average has fallen to 15 mpg. Towing—at 80 mph—will do that. The lifetime number appears to be settling around 15, which falls 4 mpg short of the EPA's 19-mpg combined rating. As a reminder, our 2019 V-8 Ram delivered 14 mpg across its entire test.

Recent findings suggest that none of this has dimmed the enthusiasm. Miller is still at peace. The logbook is still full of praise (mirrors aside). And the sign-out sheet is still full of names. The Ram 1500 is the kind of truck that makes you overlook its flaws not because they're small but because everything else is that good. Whether that's a compliment or a warning depends on how you feel about those kinds of relationships.

Months in Fleet: 11 months Current Mileage: 35,410 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $543 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0.

Let the record show that after this 20,000-mile update we are enacting a strict ban on all complaints regarding the Ram 1500's side-view mirrors. They are massive. We get it.

Yet no matter where an entry in the Ram's logbook begins, the commentary inevitably careens toward those two opaque walls of plastic and glass that often eclipse the sun, the horizon, and occasionally, entire vehicles.

It has been revealed that to wit, online production assistant Sarah Taylor was rattled after a four-way stop where the driver-side mirror successfully hid an entire sedan stopped to her left. "OMG, you can't see anything out the window," she mentioned.

Other notes since our 10,000-mile update? "I'm short," wrote managing road test editor Becca Hackett. "I look like a chicken trying to move my head around to see around that new huge blind spot.".

One writer described them as "forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas.".

Recent findings suggest that another? "Dumbo ears." If the eyes are the windows to the soul, it seems the towing mirrors are the blast shields to reality.

Industry observers note that fortunately, even the skeptics concede that once you load up a trailer and escape the confines of parking lots and city streets, the Ram settles into its role as a supreme highway cruiser. Associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald gave a "shout out to the graphic on the screen that shows exactly how much angle your steering input gives while reversing a trailer." He also admitted that "the tow mirrors were mighty useful on a seven-hour drive pulling a trailer from northeast Wisconsin." Other staffers who tow more frequently have voiced similar mirror approval, if sheepishly.

According to recent reports, it turns out judging the mirrors in a metro Detroit roundabout is like reviewing a deep-space telescope based on how well it works as a reading glass. Except you can't swap glasses because this telescope is effectively duct-taped to your face. Managing testing editor David Beard compared his experience entering a Cape Cod roundabout to a game of Russian roulette.

As we cross the halfway point of the test, small cracks begin to emerge in places other than the mirrors. We've noted a clunky 1-2 upshift and a lethargic response to downshift requests that can make city driving feel unpolished. An concern with the forward-collision system required a dealer visit to have the long-range radar module replaced (that repair was covered by the warranty). We've also caught the digital instrument cluster daydreaming: It displays a graphic of the pre-facelift Ram 1500 on multiple screens. After finishing a highway fuel-economy loop that returned 18 mpg (2 mpg better than our average thus far), road warrior Jacob Kurowicki said, "I couldn't wait to get out because of back pain.".

According to recent reports, most other comments relating to the interior have been more kind. Technical editor Mike Sutton praised the existence of analog gauges in a world where almost everything's gone digital. Ditto for the front three-across seating, which brings back childhood memories—though we remain profoundly grateful that the nostalgia stops short of locating the fuel tank behind the seatback.

But because all roads lead back to the side mirrors, they have a throwback touch of their own: They fold manually. Shutting those barn doors means getting out and walking to both sides, which is acceptable on a base trim level, but an indignity at $68,320. Sort of how you still have to fish the key fob out of your pocket to unlock the thing.

Senior editor Greg Fink noted it best: "Nix the tow mirrors, add a proximity key, and this is a near-perfect full-size truck.".

Months in Fleet: 8 months Current Mileage: 23,570 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 16 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 520 milesService: $350 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0.

In a recent development, the first 10,000 miles with a new vehicle are the exciting first dates before the mundane sets in. You're still gleefully memorizing the dashboard's contours, and the factory scent hasn't yet been fully vanquished by spilled coffee (or worse). With our long-term Ram 1500, this phase concluded with an exchange at our service department that felt less like a transaction and more like a scene from Burn After Reading.

According to recent reports, it started with an innocent request for an oil change and a cabin air filter as part of the first service dictated by the Ram's oil-life monitor. The estimate returned with two surprises. The first was the cabin air filter itself, priced at a startling $60 (the part retails for roughly half that online). The second was $17 for something called Frigi-Fresh, a disinfectant for HVAC systems.

It has been revealed that when questioned, our service advisor shrugged. Frigi-Fresh, he explained, auto-populates on the work order with every cabin air-filter replacement. By his logic, Frigi-Fresh is not an option but an inevitability.

Road warrior Jacob Kurowicki queried: "We have to tell you we don't want something that we don’t know we're going to get?".

"Look man, I just work here," the advisor noted, providing the modern-day epitaph for personal responsibility.

A memo to those patronizing Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor: Declining unwanted extras requires telepathy.

Sources indicate that the experience is the kind of thing that makes you want to change your own oil, even if it means remembering that the High-Output variant of the Hurricane engine requires 0W-40 synthetic versus the regular's 0W-20. At least the HO's special blend costs 171 percent less per ounce than Frigi-Fresh.

While it may not have the most desirable cylinder count, Ram's Hurricane twin-turbo straight-six is compelling, even if it feels as out of place in a Ram as a string quartet in a Waffle House. Stomp the gas and the soundtrack is less Woodward Avenue and more autobahn. It pulls with the confident, linear surge of something far more sophisticated.

Recent findings suggest that the six-cylinder's impressive refinement carries through to the chassis and optional air springs, which testing director Dave VanderWerp called perfect for Michigan's annual Pothole Fiesta. Consider the Ram, then, a 5765-pound limo that shrugs off road blemishes with serene detachment, making it the king of long-distance hauls. You could transport a sleeping infant in the back across a railroad crossing and the most you'd worry about is the lingering scent of Frigi-Fresh.

VanderWerp also noted that the heated cloth seats get hotter than permitted by the lawyers at other automakers, who have probably calculated the precise temperature at which a human posterior bursts into litigation.

And then there's the mirrors. We have the optional trailer tow mirrors on our truck. They stick out nearly a foot on each side, stretching 102.3 inches tip to tip. That's 8.5 feet; any wider, and you'd want a pilot car. When towing, the mirrors provide an excellent IMAX-like view of your 24-foot enclosed trailer. The other 98 percent of the time, they stick out with the unearned confidence of a cryptocurrency enthusiast, requiring geometry in fast food drive-throughs and faith-based arithmetic in roundabouts. The tow mirrors are a wonderful solution to a problem we only occasionally have.

It has been revealed that just a little more than 10,000 miles in, and our Ram has already proven itself as a brilliant, comfortable, and quick long-hauler. It's a machine so thoroughly modern that it makes you forget all about the guttural appeal of two extra cylinders. That is, right up until you're confronted with the 15 mpg we've observed so far, one measly mpg more than our result from the 2019 V-8 Ram we tested a handful of years back. And clearly we aren't alone, judging by the V-8's quick return to the 2026 order sheet. Sometimes, progress is just a detour on the way back to where you started.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 13,650 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $225 Normal Wear:$0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0.

What, another Ram? We're starting to feel like shepherds around here. This 2025 Ram 1500 Big Horn is the third Ram 1500 to undergo our 40,000-mile long-term test since 2019 (and sixth all-time), following a cushy 2019 Limited and an unhinged 2022 TRX. That's almost one every two years. So long as the Ram keeps collecting 10Best trophies (seven and counting), we'll keep inviting it back.

Industry observers note that speaking of sixes, the biggest change for this test is Ram's newly introduced six-cylinder engine. The flagship Hemi V-8? Gone from the Ram lineup entirely (for now). In its place sits the optional "Hurricane" twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six cylinder ($2695) that makes 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque. (The base engine remains a 305-hp 3.6-liter V-6.) We opted for a Massive Horn trim with six seats because we liked that symmetry.

Industry observers note that between hauling race cars to track days, towing snowmobiles to Michigan's frigid Upper Peninsula, schlepping the family to weekend sports, and the endless parade of big-screen TVs from big box stores, this Ram won't be living easy. And our team's appetite for truck utility demonstrates no signs of waning.

Sources indicate that we opted for the 33.0-gallon fuel tank ($445), which should give us plenty of range for long hauls. We're eager to see if dropping two cylinders delivers better fuel economy than the 14 mpg we observed with the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered Ram 1500 we tested in 2019.

According to recent reports, that truck was rated by the EPA at 19 mpg combined and so is this upcoming Big Horn. What's the benefit of the six-cylinder then? So far, power. In our performance testing, this Big Horn reached 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and ran the quarter-mile in 13.6 at 100 mph, eclipsing that 2019 Ram by 1.3 seconds and 1.0 second.

Industry observers note that we equipped this Ram for hauling with the Towing Technology Group ($595) and Trailer-Tow Group ($1345), which include everything from trailer-tire-pressure monitoring to side mirrors that are the size of elephant ears and boast power-adjusting convex glass. Throw in the 3.92 rear axle ($195), and we're cleared to tow 10,980 pounds and carry a 1350-pound payload.

According to recent reports, the Significant Horn Level 2 Equipment Group ($2770) brings the expected modern conveniences: a 12.0-inch infotainment touchscreen, heated front seats and steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, and so on. But in a head-scratching omission that would make a Porsche product specialist proud, passive keyless entry isn't included. Yes, our $68,320 truck requires manually hitting the unlock button on the key fob like it's 1995.

Excellent ride quality has been a longstanding attribute of the Ram 1500 thanks to its coil-spring rear suspension, which we upgraded with four-corner air springs ($1995). We can now also lower the truck to ease bed access while standing outside with the fob, which almost makes up for having to fish that fob out every time. Almost.

The Ram's interior has long set the standard for pickup luxury, though it was typically leather-lined higher-end trims earning that praise. We'll see if the excellence continues in our cloth-seat Big Horn. And we can have up to six critics weigh in on every mile.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

In a recent development, the main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

Industry observers note that it caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

It has been revealed that switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

It has been revealed that A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a big screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on noted little screen.

Regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an key thing to work on.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I stated my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

According to recent reports, with Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most important thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

And if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.

Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.

Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now introduced, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.

Industry observers note that the recent Black Ops 7 launch clearly hasn’t made many people happy, so just like Activision made Black Ops 6 free to play at BF6’s launch, EA has now done the same with its own game. The Battlefield 6 free trial, which was announced last week, is just an hour away at the time of this writing.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy released, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

The trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

It has been revealed that players will have access to four game modes, played on different versions of the same maps. Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch will all be available to choose from, and there don’t appear to be any level or XP limits in the trial.

Unfortunatley, just as the free trial was about to go live, the game got hit with a major matchmaking outage that took down all matchmaking in the core game, leaving Redsec unaffected.

Hopefully EA can resolve this glitch before the trial officially kicks off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Takata airbag recall scandal started over a decade ago. To date, some 67 million airbags have been included in that series of recalls across dozens of brands. That list is expanding again today, as Toyota is recalling another 314,000 cars in the USA. W.

In a recent development, hile the automaker hasn't spelled out exactly which models are part of the recall, owners should consider getting the fix as one of their highest priorities. According to the automaker, the new recall of 314,000 cars affects both Toyota and Lexus products. The tech giant did not break down the make and year models impacted, but the brand says that in all affected vehicles, the issue is consistent with previous Takata recalls. The inflator in the airbag has a propellant inside that can degrade over time due to humidity and temperature fluctuations.

If that inflator ruptures due to that degradation, it can send metal fragments through the airbag and into the cabin. Takata airbags impacted by this issue have injured and killed people over the years. Perhaps the biggest concern is that there is no warning sign of when this might happen.

Sources indicate that toyota says it'll replace the front passenger airbag inflator or the entire assembly depending on the model. While we do not have a make and model list, Toyota does say that owners can cross-check their VIN at Toyota.com/recall or at NHTSA.gov/recalls. In the coming days, we'll likely see the formal documents published by the NHTSA with specifics.

In a recent development, it is worth noting that recalls like this don't necessarily suggest that Toyota was installing faulty airbags recently. According to the NHTSA, 9% of the bad airbags that went out into the automotive population are still out there. That might not sound like much, but that small sliver still accounts for over six million cars. Based on the latest available data, the 2017 Lexus GX460 was the most recent Toyota product included in Takata recalls. Other notable models include the 2008-2014 Lexus IS F, the 2010-2016 Toyota 4Runner, and the 2012 Lexus LFA.

According to recent reports, the ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the fresh ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.

According to recent reports, following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it.

The new electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.

Recent findings suggest that volkswagen revealed on Thursday that series production of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.

“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer remarked last month after unveiling the newly introduced SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”.

The ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.

Sources indicate that volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The new design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.

Unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the newly introduced ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.

In Volkswagen’s words, the upcoming ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”.

Recent findings suggest that inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s new infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.

In a recent development, another highlight is the return of physical buttons. After listening to customer feedback from current drivers, Volkswagen added physical buttons under the center display and on the steering wheel for climate control and other vehicle functions.

To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun newly introduced Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.

Drivers can also choose from six classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.

In a recent development, the fresh Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:.

Depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “upcoming benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.

After it launches in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen remarked the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.

Industry observers note that apparently, the new ID Tiguan has a slightly better Cx (Drag Coefficient) at 0.26 versus 0.28 on first gen ID4 and 0.27 on 2nd gen. According to VW, it’s achieved using front air curtains, a minimal air intake, an enclosed underbody, and a longer roof spoiler.

Volkswagen said prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.

Since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.

Official US prices have not yet been announced. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

#5233. 8 Metroidvanias Where Every Choice Matters

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

8 Metroidvanias Where Every Choice Matters

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Choice one of the mechanics that does a lot to set video games apart from other forms of media, and can take many different forms.
  • Metroidvanias focus primarily on exploration, abilities, and exploration, and there are plenty of games in the genre that take things a step further by giving you meaningful decisions that influence your adventure.
  • UNSIGHTED includes a game mechanic that makes choice one of its most notable features.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choice one of the mechanics that does a lot to set video games apart from other forms of media, and can take many different forms. It’s what draws me to RPGs, but even genres that aren’t known for their story choices like Metroidvanias have choice play some kind of a role, even if it’s something like how you build your character and approach combat.

Metroidvanias focus primarily on exploration, abilities, and exploration, and there are plenty of games in the genre that take things a step further by giving you meaningful decisions that influence your adventure. Even within this framework, choice matters as builds, abilities, weapons, and exploration all play a role. These are Metroidvanias where those choices play a bigger role than is typical of the genre.

UNSIGHTED includes a game mechanic that makes choice one of its most notable features. Characters, including yours, are all on a time limit before they disappear, or become “unsighted”. Your time can be extended thanks to meteor dust, a limited resource that forces you to decide who gets to live and who has to die.

This turns resource management into a moral dilemma, particularly because your decisions have consequences beyond individual character interactions. Saving certain NPCs can preserve access to shops, quests, and useful items, while allowing others to become unsighted can permanently change what you have access to. It's a clever way of making your decisions feel important without relying exclusively on dialogue options or branching cutscenes. Every time you discover a upcoming character, you have another difficult decision to make on the horizon.

Sources indicate that death’s Gambit: Afterlife has a lot of RPG elements with a strong Metroidvania influence, which puts it in an awkward in-between category. But, because of this, choice is more key here than is typical of Metroidvanias. It features multiple endings, with some of the most important decisions tied to your encounters with Death and Thalamus. Depending on your progression and the decisions you make during the adventure, you'll have opportunities to pursue different narrative outcomes.

I particularly like games that connect RPG mechanics to storytelling in this way. Rather than treating character development as something that exists independently of the main narrative, Death's Gambit: Afterlife makes your progression part of the decision-making process.

It has been revealed that nine Sols is already great if you're looking for a challenging Metroidvania that comes with a good story. It also goes the extra mile by making the relationships that you develop throughout the game incredibly relevant, and unlocks a different ending.

In a recent development, you’ll encounter several characters who join you at the Four Seasons Pavilion, most notably Shuanshuan and Shennong. Both these characters introduce questlines that require you to invest time in helping them. Completing these quests, alongside other optional discoveries, is necessary to unlock the game's Shooting Star Ending, also known as the True Ending. Having a reason to invest in a game’s characters, beyond it being its own reward, is an example of game design done well, and it means that the ending you get is influenced by the choice you make to invest in them.

Blasphemous 2 is a particularly good example of a Metroidvania that rewards you for looking beyond its main storyline. While exploring Cvstodia, you'll encounter numerous optional challenges, hidden collectibles, and characters with their own stories to uncover.

Some of these discoveries are particularly important if you want to unlock the game's true ending. It makes the choice to explore and complete side quests more important, and neglecting them means getting the less satisfactory ending. What's interesting is that you can technically reach the final encounter without completing any of the side objectives. However, doing so means missing out on an entirely different conclusion.

One of Salt and Sanctuary’s more interesting mechanics involves the different Creeds you can pledge allegiance to throughout the game. Creeds offer different benefits, resources, and services, meaning your allegiance can influence how you approach progression. Choosing to follow one Creed over another can affect which items and services are available to you, while interacting with rival sanctuaries can have consequences of their own.

You can also choose how to develop your character, with an extensive skill tree and a wide variety of weapons, armour, and spells allowing you to experiment with different builds. While its choices are more closely tied to character progression and faction allegiance than branching narrative decisions, Salt and Sanctuary still gives you plenty of opportunities to change your adventure based on your choices.

Vigil: The Longest Night is another dark fantasy Metroidvania that takes inspiration from Soulslike games and Salt and Sanctuary. You play as Leila, a warrior tasked with investigating the strange events affecting her homeland. As you explore, you'll encounter characters who have their own problems, motivations, and quests to complete.

In a recent development, one Vigil’s more interesting aspects is how its optional content encourages you to investigate the circumstances surrounding the people you encounter. Rather than simply following the main storyline, you can spend time helping NPCs and uncovering additional information about the world. The game also features multiple endings, giving you additional reasons to investigate its mysteries and pursue optional content. There’s a lot of character and environmental story here, and your experience is largely shaped by your decisions.

In a recent development, ENDER LILIES: Quietus of the Knights is a particularly atmospheric Metroidvania that follows Lily, a young priestess attempting to uncover the truth behind a devastating plague known as the Blight. As you explore the ruined kingdom, you'll encounter the spirits of fallen warriors who can help Lily in combat. Each spirit has its own abilities, allowing you to experiment with different combinations and develop a combat style that suits your preferences, bringing choice into play.

Alongside its gameplay, choice also plays a massive part in its endings, with three possible outcomes. The best outcome involves thoroughly exploring and finding all seven Stone Tablet Fragments, which allows you to craft the Liminant Aegis Curio, an artifact that protects Lily. It neatly ties together narrative with exploration, and gives more incentive for exploration.

Infernax is one of the best examples of a Metroidvania where your decisions have consequences. This is because of a morality system, which always makes a game that is influenced by your choices. The morality system is determined by how you choose to help the people of your kingdom. Infernax gives you multiple options with how to deal with situations, and with both noble and selfish options available.

According to recent reports, in addition to affecting your alignment, your choices also determine which ending you’ll receive. Infernax is a fantastic example of a game that gives you the freedom to shape your character's journey.

#5232. How to Become Change-Curious

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1100 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How to Become Change-Curious

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station).
  • What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning fresh ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food plans, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

Given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

Industry observers note that noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

It has been revealed that looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

According to recent reports, shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a new instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

According to recent reports, sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a upcoming behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Sources indicate that curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.
